title: How an Inside Buyout Saved This 35-Year-Old Richmond Jewelry Store
text: Share Tweet Carrying the Torch Forward How Caitie Sellers and Maggie Smith honored a retiring owner's legacy — and grew sales 72%. Published 2 days ago on April 30, 2026 By Chris Burslem Instore May 2026 Issue Dransfield Jewelers, Richmond, VA OWNERS: Caitie Sellers and Maggie Smith; digital presence: 64 5-Star Google reviews; 2,000 Instagram followers; FOUNDED: 1991; Opened featured location: 1991; AREA: 1,400 square feet; DESIGN: Mariya Boykova and Daniel Ricky Furniture; BRANDS: More than 20 independent artists; EMPLOYEES: 1 full-time, 2 part-time WHEN DON DRANSFIELD decided to retire in 2022 after three decades of running his jewelry shop in Richmond’s leafy Shockoe Slip district, his plan was simply to close it and move on. His store manager and goldsmith, Caitie Sellers, convinced him otherwise — proposing instead that she bring in a partner with additional management experience to buy the business and keep it going. This inside “takeover” explains much about how Dransfield operates today, with Sellers and Maggie Smith building on Don’s legacy of craftsmanship and community-minded customer service, developing a modern jeweler that caters well to Richmond’s knowledgeable local jewelry market. “Don trusted his staff, and he gave every customer the same attention, from brand-new faces to 30-year patrons,” Sellers recalls. When he retired, she says, he told them he trusted them to take care of his name — “and to have a good time.” They have. Sales are up 72 percent from 2023 to 2025. The store now employs three goldsmiths — one more than before — to keep pace with demand. Caitie Sellers and Maggie Smith Room for Art The store’s 1,400-square-foot space on a cobblestone stretch of Shockoe Slip underwent a full renovation in 2023, designed in collaboration with interior designer Mariya Boykova and Daniel Ricky Furniture. The goals were practical as much as aesthetic: improve traffic flow, brighten the space, and raise the display cases to allow for side-by-side selling — a subtle but meaningful shift away from the traditional across-the-counter dynamic. The result has its own distinct personality. White walls and ceilings open up the main showroom, while custom-built showcases in pink and chartreuse — what Smith calls the store’s “sparkles” — give it warmth and color. Large woven rattan light fixtures hang overhead. The historic bones of the building, including its wood floors, remain intact. The most distinctive feature is a former recessed archway that has been converted into what the owners call “The Jewelry Box” — a dedicated exhibition space for contemporary jewelry artists. Roughly 6 by 7 feet, the nook hosts six rotating installations a year, some wired for sound, featuring work from national and international artists. The store held its first juried exhibit there in 2023, with eight artists from seven states. It functions as a gallery as much as a retail space, and that’s intentional. Dransfield represents 20 independent studio jewelers and carries no brands. The Jewelry Box is an extension of that philosophy — a way to showcase conceptual work that pushes against the boundaries of traditional jewelry design, in a setting where someone might also be shopping for an engagement ring. PATRON OF THE ARTS. Dransfield sponsors the Excellence in Jewelry award at The Visual Arts Center of Richmond’s annual Craft + Design show. The Engine Room Downstairs, in a basement workshop, the store’s goldsmiths handle every piece that comes through — custom designs, repairs, restorations. Nothing is outsourced. Sellers came to the partnership with a background in both jewelry-making and business ownership; she had worked for Don as store manager and bookkeeper before the transition. Smith brought customer service, curation, and employee management. Together, their skills covered most of what a full-service jewelry operation requires. The remaining gaps — insurance, security, landlord negotiations — turned out to be the steeper learning curve. “Certain aspects of operating a brick-and-mortar business were very new and challenging,” Smith says. Custom design now accounts for the majority of the store’s sales. Clients can consult directly with the goldsmiths working on their pieces, whether that’s a new commission or a family heirloom brought in for restoration. A former recessed archway, converted into “The Jewelry Box,” hosts six rotating exhibitions a year of work by jewelry artists. In the Community Dransfield’s community ties are broad and specific. The store collaborates with Virginia Commonwealth University’s Craft and Material Studies program, hosting student sales and providing technical examples for coursework. It sponsors the Excellence in Jewelry award at The Visual Arts Center of Richmond’s annual Craft + Design show, and participated in the 2024 “Jewels for Children” raffle, which raised $26,000 for art therapy programs at the Children’s Hospital Foundation. Smith is also on the board of the Baltimore Jewelry Center, a nonprofit focusing on the support of makers & art jewelry in the United States and internationally. The store is pet-friendly, which in Shockoe Slip is less a gimmick than a natural extension of what the neighborhood values. Richmond’s arts community, Smith notes, gives the city’s jewelry market a particular character — one that makes a store like Dransfield a better fit than it might be elsewhere. The VCU connection reflects that: a pipeline between academic craft culture and the commercial world, with a shared emphasis on handwork and material knowledge. Advertisement Modernizing Without Losing the Thread Asked what she’d tell other independent retailers considering a similar renovation or ownership transition, Smith advocates keeping it grounded. “We think it’s important to honor the roots of the original business. Pinpoint why your customers have kept coming back and recommending their friends — in our case, providing careful, honest, and expert services, and keep that at the heart of your business. It is possible to retain the store’s values while modernizing the business if you are mindful in your decisions as you update.” Five Cool Things About Dransfield Jewelers 1. The “Jewelry Box” Gallery. A small nook serves as a dedicated exhibition space for conceptual art jewelry. Hosting six annual exhibitions, the “Box” features site-specific installations—sometimes even wired for sound—to showcase work from national and international artists. Participating artists often show more wearable work in the main cases alongside their installation, letting clients move between conceptual and everyday jewelry in the same visit. 2. Campus Connection. Dransfield has an active relationship with Virginia Commonwealth University’s nationally recognized Craft and Material Studies program — hosting student sales, providing real-world technical examples for coursework, and supporting group exhibitions of student and alumni work. One semester, a VCU professor assigned students extra credit for visiting the store to study specific jewelry-making techniques in the showcases. 3. Engine Room. No outsourcing here. Dransfield maintains a full-service workshop in its basement. Clients can speak directly with the goldsmiths designing their engagement rings or restoring family heirlooms, ensuring a transparent and deeply personal “modern heirloom” creation process. Advertisement 4. The Window. The storefront on East Cary Street changes with the seasons — strings of autumn leaves in fall, fairy lights in winter — giving the hunter-green façade a handmade, neighborhood-scale presence on the cobblestone block. Inside, the same spirit carries through: Persian rugs on wood floors, woven rattan pendant lights overhead, pink-and-chartreuse showcases and sparkle icons that are painted on the walls. 5. Giving Back. The store’s 2024 “Jewels for Children” raffle raised $26,000 for art therapy programs at the Children’s Hospital Foundation. Beyond that single event, Dransfield participates in local repair cafés, sponsors the Excellence in Jewelry award at The Visual Arts Center of Richmond’s annual Craft + Design show, and contributes to silent auctions for community organizations. PHOTO GALLERY (9 IMAGES) JUDGES’ COMMENTS Larry Johnson: The traditional outside face of the store is pure historic Richmond, then you open the door and the colorful interior is a great surprise. Duvall O’Steen: Love the colorful showcases — feels contemporary, like a fun place to shop. Love the community connections and the “repair cafés” or “mending days” — great way to identify the store’s commitment to custom jewelry and repair/renovation of meaningful heirlooms. Dianna Rae High: The Jewelry Box nook dedicated to showcasing conceptual art jewelry is a brilliant idea. Anna Samsonova: Love the pop-up artist arch! Jennifer Shaheen: The store celebrates both legacy and forward-thinking creativity. They’re redefining what jewelry retail can be: artful, inclusive, and deeply personal. Danielle Marzarella: Dransfield’s blends legacy and modern design in a really thoughtful way. The renovated space is bright, open, and approachable, with custom fixtures and creative displays that reflect their craftsmanship and artistic point of view.
